title: MB0-07335
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant is XXXX XXXX. He is a XXXX-year old citizen of Hungary. He is Roma. He is claiming refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The claimant is Roma. He alleges that he has suffered persecution in Hungary because of being Roma. He was threatened and spit on and the police did not help him.
The claimant came to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2010 and claimed refugee protection.
The panel concludes that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" nor is he a "person in need of protection."
The panel is satisfied as to the identity of the claimant on the basis of his Hungarian passport on record.

The determinative issue in this case was state protection. The panel also examined whether the incidents of discrimination experienced by the claimant in Hungary because of his Roma ethnicity would amount to persecution when considered singularly or cumulatively.

The claimant lived in the small town of XXXX where 30% of the population is Roma. The claimant described that the most fearful incident in his life occurred when he was at a bus stop in XXXX and a group of skinheads attacked him and that this occurred in the summer of 2010. They spit on him and struck him but he managed to get away. The claimant testified that he went to report the incident to the police the next day, but had been told that they could not do anything since he did not know the identities of his aggressors. The claimant had also waited until the next day to make his report. Later in the hearing, the claimant testified that two months after the incident he had received a report from the police stating that the investigation was now closed.

The claimant's PIF had mentioned being spit on. However in his PIF he had stated that he went to the police but that they had refused to fill out a report. From the claimant's testimony it appears that the police took his report and also took the copy of the medical report. However considering the fact that the claimant had waited a day to file his report and had not known his attackers, the police subsequently closed the investigation because they had nothing to go on.

From the claimant's testimony it appears that the police took his report and did not ignore or refuse to fill out a report. The actions of the police were well within what would be considered reasonable in the circumstances. The panel notes that random assaults are difficult to investigate and protect against and even the most effective, well-resourced and highly motivated police forces will have difficulty providing effective protection.1 The state may not always be successful in protecting its citizens but as long as it makes serious efforts to do so, this will generally suffice.2

The claimant had been asked if there had been another incident after that attack in the summer of 2010. He replied that there had not been. However, he went on to describe an event in the fall of 2010, when the car in which he was in had been shaken by a group of skinheads. He described that a police car had been in the area and that the two officers inside had spoken to the skinheads. The claimant and his friends had gone to a nearby coffee shop. They had then asked the police to escort them out of the village and he testified that the police car escorted them for about five to six kilometres until they were safely outside the village.

The claimant also reported having the windshield of his car broken by a skinhead with a baseball bat and stated that this had occurred in XXXX 2010. Asked why he had stated earlier in the hearing that there were no other events after the summer of 2010, the claimant then said that he did not consider these serious.

The claimant stated in his PIF that on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2010, he had gone to the local police station but that the police had done nothing. The claimant stated that it was because he had seen skinheads in the forest near his home and he was afraid. The claimant however had testified that he had first noticed these skinheads in the forest in the spring of 2010 and had seen them there about eight times. He stated that on five occasions he and other villagers had gone to the Mayor's office to do something about the situation. The mayor had responded by sending a patrol of volunteer citizens out and that he had done this on two occasions.

The claimant said that the town of XXXX was located just 20 kilometres away from his village and that the Roma were being shot and killed in that village. The claimant stated that this began at the beginning of 2010. The documentary evidence however states that the trouble in XXXX occurred in XXXX 2011, after the claimant was already in Canada.3 When asked if there were similar problems in his village, the claimant answered that he was not aware of anything. The claimant had mentioned that because of the strategic location of his house, his house was targeted by the skinheads, yet when asked if his home had been attacked before he left Hungary, the claimant stated that it had not. Asked if he had heard about anything happening to his house since he left, he said he was not aware of anything.

The claimant stated that about 15 to 20 people had left from his village to come to Canada and that when he arrived in Canada he stayed with a friend from his village, who had come to Canada several months before.

The panel examined the possibility of adequate state protection for the claimant in Hungary. In assessing the issue of state protection, the panel is guided by a number of cases. There is a presumption that the state is capable of protecting its citizens, except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown.4 To rebut the presumption of state protection, the claimant must present clear and convincing evidence, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.

Claimants from a democratic country have a heavy burden when attempting to show that they should not have been required to exhaust all of the recourses available to them domestically before claiming refugee status. The documentary evidence shows that Hungary is a functioning democracy5. The burden of proving an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy that exists in the state.6 Hungary has functioning political and judicial systems in place, and an official apparatus sufficient to provide a measure of protection to its citizens. Hungary is in control of its territory and has functioning security forces in place. There is no evidence of a total breakdown of state authority in the country. Therefore, the burden of attempting to show that one should not be required to exhaust all avenues of domestic recourse is a heavy one.7

In order to determine whether the claimant has discharged his burden of proof, the panel considered whether the state of Hungary is capable of providing protection and willing to act. In Carrillo8 the Federal Court of Appeal stated that the refugee claimant who claims that state protection is inadequate bears the evidentiary burden of adducing evidence to that effect. The onus to rebut the presumption of state protection remains at all times on the refugee claimant.9 The panel is of the opinion that the claimant has failed to do so. After the most serious incident in the summer of 2010 the police took his report and investigated although they were forced to close the file because of lack of evidence and any information as to who the aggressors were. The claimant had no knowledge who his aggressors were and had furthermore, gone to report the attack to the police only on the following day.

While the documentary evidence in the National Documentation Package on the treatment of Roma in Hungary states that in recent years there have been attacks against the Roma, the documentary evidence also reports that following these recent attacks against the Roma, the government has acted to protect its citizens of Roma origin. For example, the government created a special group of 100 police officers to investigate cases believed to be linked and offered a reward for useful information on these attacks against the Roma. Police also reinforced their presence in nearly 200 small communities to protect citizens from further violence. The National Police also held two regional conferences to inform Romani leaders about progress in the investigations and to seek new ways to prevent discrimination and anti-Romani crime in Romani communities. Amnesty International 2011 reports that the police completed its investigation into the series of attacks against the Roma which occurred in 2008 and 2009 and that four suspects had been charged as a result10.

The documentary evidence states that the fascist paramilitary group known as the Hungarian Guard was reportedly banned in 2009 by the Hungarian courts for "rejecting equal rights to Romas and inciting resentment against them."11 The panel is aware that the group reorganized itself into new organizations with similar-sounding names and many of the same members. While right wing extremist groups do exist in Hungary, an article in the National Documentation Package discusses state response to the attacks against Roma individuals by fascist groups. As mentioned earlier the Hungarian Guard was banned in 2009. In 2011, the Hungarian government proposed changes to the Penal Code in part to deal with the spate of street marches by groups of people dressed in 'non-official uniforms'. In May 2011, the Hungarian Parliament adopted an amendment to the Criminal Code to protect the Roma community from "extreme right-wing groups." The amendment, which was a response to events involving right-wing groups dressed in uniforms, reportedly extends hate crimes legislation to include intimidation of ethnic, racial and religious or other groups. Furthermore, a 2011 Hungarian government report to the United Nations states that, in order to "prosecute the illegal activity of people not willing to acknowledge" the Hungarian Guard's court-ordered dissolution, there is: legislation ordered to prosecute participation in the activities of the dissolved social organization as an infringement of the law. The law prosecutes even wearing clothes that resemble to the uniform, usual attire of the dissolved social organization and makes it possible to impose even custodial sentences.

According to the Political Handbook of the World 2011, in 2009, police doubled the size of a task force investigating anti-Roma attacks. In July 2009, police banned a demonstration that was to be held on Szabadsag Square in Budapest and the police indicated that they would "take firm action against any private individual or member of any organization, with special regard to the Hungarian Guard" who want to demonstrate. In April 2010, charges were filed with the public prosecutor against the chief of the Hungarian Guard and two of his associates on "suspicion of illegally maintaining the uniformed organization". The AP similarly reported that on the same day, police filed charges against three leaders of the Hungarian Guard. Because the group was still operating in spite of its ban, the charges also included "incitement against authorities' decrees". Nine days later, MTI-EcoNews reported that police filed charges against ten leaders of the banned Hungarian Guard for violating the laws of assembly. In July 2010, police arrested more than 70 members of the Hungarian National Guard at demonstrations in Budapest that were attended by around 600 members of the organization to commemorate the banning of the Hungarian Guard. Police also arrested another 20 Hungarian National Guard members attending the same rallies because they were in possession of minor firearms.

Furthermore the documentary evidence states that in Hungary there is an Independent Board that had been created to deal with complaints against the police. The documentary evidence states the following: In 2008, an Independent Board for complaints against the police was created to "investigate concrete complaints against the actions of police" This Board is composed of five legal experts elected by Parliament for 6 years. The Board is an independent body that offers viewpoints to the police on decisions taken and provides "recommendations to improve the work of the Police12. This organization investigates violations and omissions by the police that affected fundamental human rights.

The panel concludes that if at any time the claimant had gone to the police and had the police not provided him with any assistance, he would have been able to make a complaint to this organization. The panel finds that in the instances that the claimant described the police did offer protection, such as the time that they escorted the claimant and his friends out of a village to ensure their protection.

The claimant is Roma and the panel examined the documentary evidence on the situation of the Roma in Hungary. The documentary evidence contains a 60-page European Commission Against Racism and Intolerance (ECRI) report on Hungary13, which discusses the Roma minority and their situation and states that their situation of disadvantage is such that long-term but intensive efforts will be needed to turn it around. While many of the measures taken to date may have a positive impact, they need to be continued and in some cases intensified. In June 2007, Parliament approved a resolution on the Decade of Roma Inclusion Program Strategic Plan, setting a framework for action in a series of fields where Roma experience discrimination and disadvantage in daily life. Wide-ranging measures have been taken in the field of education and some landmark decisions of the courts have been handed down in recent years. On the basis of the report, it appears that Hungary is providing concrete solutions to the difficulties which the Roma are experiencing.

Most ministries have special officers for Romani affairs focused on the needs of the Romani community. The government in Hungary has provided programs assisting Roma in further education, and most ministries and county labour affairs centers had special officers for Romani affairs focused on the needs of the Romani community.14 One example is the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour, which established a Department for Roma Integration, which "pays attention to the enhancement of the labour market opportunities of the Roma population, operates a scholarship scheme for the young Roma, and cooperates with organisations for the protection of the rights and interests of Roma people."15

Sources state that the Hungarian government has taken a number of legal and institutional measures to improve the situation of the Roma minority16. Funds were allocated to various ministries and local governments for programs supporting Romani integration. The Hungarian Government lists a number of institutions within the state apparatus, including the Roma Integration Department within the Ministry of Social Affairs and Labour, the main government body responsible for Romani integration and the Council of Roma Integration, a "consultative, advisory body," which coordinates measures between various ministries on the social inclusion of Roma. The Inter-ministerial Committee on Roma Affairs is a government body headed by the leader of the Romani self-government that coordinates state tasks pertaining to Roma issues.

The claimant had mentioned in his PIF that as a Roma store clerks refused to serve him because he was Roma. The Equal Treatment Authority (ETA) is an independent organization established by the Hungarian government that is tasked with investigating complaints of discrimination against public bodies such as the police, military, municipalities, and schools in the fields of employment, education, access to goods or any other field. Between 2005 and 2006, approximately 30 percent of cases handled by the ETA concerned Roma. The ETA may take various actions against an offending body, such as ordering it to cease its discriminatory practice, publicizing the result of an investigation or imposing fines. For example, in 2007, the ETA imposed a 600,000 forint fine on a pizzeria that had placed a sign outside its doors stating "We don't serve Gypsies". had the claimant suffered discrimination he could have made a complaint to this organization.

To be considered persecution, the mistreatment suffered or anticipated must be serious 17 and in order to determine whether particular mistreatment would qualify as "serious" it is necessary to examine what interest of the claimant might be harmed and to what extent the subsistence, employment, expression or exercise of that interest may be compromised. This approach has been approved in the courts, which have equally equated the notion of a serious compromising of interest with a key denial of a core human right.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Handbook, which although not binding, has been considered by the Supreme Court of Canada to be a persuasive authority, provides as follows: No. 54. Differences in the treatment of various groups do indeed exist to a greater or lesser extent in many societies. Persons who receive less favourable treatment as a result of such differences are not necessarily victims of persecution. It is only in certain circumstances that discrimination will amount to persecution. 18

This would be so if measures of discrimination lead to consequences of a substantially prejudiced nature for the person concerned, i.e. serious restrictions on the right to earn a livelihood, practice his religion, access reasonable employment to provide a living for himself, or to access healthcare or education. This is not so in the present case.

The claimant worked throughout his lifetime. He described working for nine years in Budapest and five years for the XXXX XXXX Company in Budapest. When asked when this had been he stated that it was in 1985. His response to question 7 in his PIF however, had indicated that he had worked there form 1999 until 2007. The claimant had stated that things in Hungary got significantly worse after the year 2000. Yet his PIF indicated that he was working in those years. Asked to explain the discrepancy as to why he had stated that he worked for XXXX XXXX company in 1985 when his PIF had mentioned working there from 1999 until 2007, the claimant then said it was possible that it may have been those years that he had indicated there.

The claimant also obtained a job in his village of XXXX in 2009 and worked there until his departure to Canada. While he alleged he was discriminated against and only three or four Romas worked for the company, the claimant had been hired by the company despite his Roma origin and had been recommended to his employer by a non-Roma friend.

The panel considered the alleged incidents which, if taken individually, do not amount to persecution, but if taken together, may justify a claim to a well-founded fear of persecution, but did not conclude this to be the case. The claimant was employed. He had his own home which he built with his parents and the house had electricity and water.

After examining the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel notes that although prejudices still exist in Hungary against the Roma and problems with fascists groups exist, the Hungarian government has put initiatives in place to eradicate stereotypes and help victims of discriminatory acts and also to curb the violence from right-wing organizations. The panel finds that the government of Hungary has solid measures in place to adequately deal with the situation of the disadvantaged Roma and to fight racism.

The Protocol on Asylum for Nationals of Member States of the European Union states that given the level of protection of fundamental rights and freedoms by the Member States of the European Union, Member States shall be regarded as constituting safe countries of origin with respect to each other for all legal and practical purposes in relation to asylum matters19. This protocol effectively disqualifies EU nationals from claiming asylum in the EU as all the current EU-member states are designated as safe countries of origin and most EU nations regard the Protocol as binding and enforce its measures.

The panel notes that Hungary is a responsible member of the European Union and reports regularly to the governance structures within that Union. Hungary is therefore responsible for upholding a number of various standards to maintain its membership in the Union. For instance, the European Commission against Racism and Intolerance (ECRI) was established by the Council of Europe and it is an independent human rights monitoring body specialized in questions relating to racism and intolerance. It is composed of independent and impartial members, who are appointed on the basis of their moral authority and recognized expertise in dealing with racism, xenophobia, anti-Semitism and intolerance. The ECRI published a report on Hungary in which it gives praise to Hungary for its accomplishments, cites issues of concern, and gives recommendation for future action.20 Hungary is taking the measures to implement the standards that are mandated as a member of the European Union. Hungary, as an EU member, will be expected to take seriously the recommendations of the different European commissions that monitor the situation of the Roma.

The panel finds that the Hungarian state is making efforts to improve the situation of the Roma and it appears that the state can adequately protect its Roma citizens. While discrimination does still exist, particularly in housing, employment and education, the government has passed laws to address the situation and has funded initiatives to implement the laws. When laws are violated charges and prosecution follow and it appears that the police are being held accountable for their actions if they fail to take Roma complaints seriously or become agents of persecution of Roma citizens themselves. Investigations, charges and convictions have been noted even when the accused are police officers. There is a legal structure in place that gives victims redress to the rule of law.

For these reasons, the panel finds that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" as he would not face a serious possibility of persecution in Hungary today. The panel finds that the claimant is not a "person in need of protection" as his removal, on a balance of probabilities, would not subject him personally to the dangers and risks stipulated in paragraphs 97(1) (a) and (b) of the Act.

The panel finds that the claimant, XXXX XXXX, is not a "Convention refugee" nor is he a "person in need of protection". His claim is rejected.
